Senses.Explanation: The matter has no single fixed direction is a formal pivot in Chan addresses: after denying that fixed talk, questions, or verbal display can contain the matter, the cited hall speaker opens another line for questioning or provisional speech. Jianfu Chenggu says the matter has no single direction before opening it eight ways for the assembly. Xingyang Qingpou rejects talk about Chan and question-answer traffic, then pairs the phrase with 'principle comes out by a hundred paths' and invites questions. Fayun Datong Shanben uses it before admitting the ancestors' second-order gate and speaking east and west. Fotuo Xun uses it to qualify his denial that verbal performance can transmit the matter. The recurrent job is an explicit pivot, not a claim that every direction is equivalent.

Senses.Explanation: Disciplinary rules are the hard forms that regulate conduct; Chan records preserve them as rules that can be received, followed, broken, or falsely dismissed in the name of freedom. Zhongfeng Mingben criticizes people who break the disciplinary rules and violate prohibitions without fear, then later rejects the opposite error of making secondary observance into a fixed mechanism. His two warnings keep the rule hard without making it the whole Chan test. Zhuanyu Guanheng explicitly glosses the title Daily Disciplinary Rules as the ordinary forms for maintaining conduct in daily use so it is not lost. In a raised case, Shakyamuni Buddha says two monastics have violated the disciplinary rules; Poshan Haiming then reworks how their expulsion and the subsequent request for teaching would be handled. Biographies also record receiving, following, or refusing such rules as concrete acts rather than abstract category.

Senses.Note: It is not generic cultivation, and praise in one biography does not define every rule.

The compound occurs 760 times in 193 allowlisted texts. Nanquan's biography identifies him as Puyuan, a son of the Wang family of Zhengzhou, and immediately records him saying, 'Old Master Wang is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy?' Other self-references include the water-buffalo saying, 'Old Master Wang has raised a water buffalo since he was young,' asking Zhaozhou, 'Where is Old Master Wang at fault?' and saying that Old Master Wang, unlike Mazu, does not say 'mind is buddha' but 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing.' Later comments preserve the title while explicitly naming Nanquan.

Senses.Explanation: To see one's own nature. Chan records place this claim in transmission formulas, instructions, questions, and explicit challenges. Hongren links it with directly becoming a buddha; a text attributed to Bodhidharma says that seeking a buddha requires it. Huangbo Xiyun answers a direct question by refusing to make nature a second object seen by a separate seeing subject. Dahui Zonggao repeats that it is required for an unerring road and immediately asks which mind recognizes and which nature is seen. Zhongfeng Mingben says direct pointing is no longer direct once it enters speech or contrivance, while Yongming Yanshou says that once nature is seen, mind and the teaching remedies both cease. The phrase names a claimed recognition, but the records repeatedly test what the grammar of a seer looking at a separate nature would wrongly add.

Senses.Explanation: The four ordinary functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, named together as a fixed sequence. Chan texts warn against constructing an additional understanding from them or treating some separate entity as standing behind them. The same functions can be described as the cause of birth and death and, without changing the wording, as the root of release. Other passages say that they neither obstruct complete command nor bind a person in themselves. Translate the four actions directly; do not replace them with an imported technical noun such as 'awareness.'

Senses.Explanation: Seeing the tracks is the second oxherding stage: the seeker has found signs of the ox but has not yet caught it. Oxherding sequences place it after seeking the ox and before seeing or catching the ox. Their headings, prefaces, and verses describe tracks beside water or in wild country as an initial but incomplete disclosure. The stage explanations explicitly call it provisional and distinguish seeing traces from direct possession. The corpus's own sequence fixes the stage's observable job.

Senses.Note: Two exact works use seeing traces outside the oxherding-stage title, once for traces appearing with mental turning and once for traces that remain after knowing where to return.

Senses.Explanation: The recorded formula “Open your mouth and you are already wrong” is spoken as both self-verdict and interview challenge, commonly paired with losing by silence or missing as soon as the mind frames an answer. Literally, open the mouth and immediately or already be wrong : "open your mouth and you are already wrong." The phrase occurs 43 times in 34 allowlisted texts; the variant "open your mouth and it is then wrong" occurs 13 times in 10. Its early defining exchange has an unnamed questioner ask Dabe to speak apart from removing the upper and taking away the lower. Dabe answers, "when I open my mouth I am already wrong" . The unnamed questioner calls Dabe his guide; Dabe replies, "today I died in the disciple's hands" , so the record shows the verdict catching Dabe’s own utterance. Later masters make it a portable paired formula: Po'an says, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; aim the mind and you immediately miss" . Other records pair it with "move a thought and immediately go against" . Wuzhun states the closed-mouth counterpart, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; close your mouth and you are already lost," then asks how communication is possible apart from opening and not opening . The phrase also becomes an encounter instruction: Baishan tells an unnamed questioner, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; move a thought and immediately go against; leave these two roads and speak quickly!" The unnamed questioner answers, "wrong," and Baishan answers with another stock retort. Chan thus bends an ordinary judgment of erroneous speech into a self-applying verdict, a fixed parallel line, and a demand used while requiring an answer; the records preserve the resulting replies rather than defining silence as the solution.

Senses.Explanation: To disclose or show something, including instruction shown in a public interview. An unnamed monk asks Baizhang Yuansu to disclose the intention of the patriarch’s coming from the west and receives “the mud ox swallows the huge wave”; the named layman He Changbai asks Juelang Daosheng for instruction for the Fushan assembly and receives a verse about clouds and snow. In the Longtan–Tianhuang case, Longtan Chongxin complains that he has long attended without being shown the essentials of mind. Tianhuang Daowu lists raising a hand when tea was brought and lowering his head when greeted, then asks, “Where was I not showing you the essentials of mind?” (那裏不是與你開示心要處). The Blue Cliff Record's compiler narrates that Jingqing Daofu used a responsive dynamic to “show later students” (開示後學); Jingqing is the person described, not the utterer of that clause. The monastery manager Chengyi tells Jifei Ruyi that he has received Jifei’s disclosure (承師開示), treating Jifei’s reply as instruction already given. Request, act, repeated conduct, and received instruction are stages of the same showing, not different lexical referents.
